topic: The 5G Carrier Race That Reshuffled Everything
description: A timeline comparison of how China’s telecom juggernaut scale, Ericsson’s infrastructure footing, and Nokia’s comeback attempt played out as 5G rollouts accelerated (and spectrum/competition shocks hit).

instagram_caption:
🚀 The 5G Carrier Race That Reshuffled Everything… and it wasn’t even close.

In the mid-2010s, 5G wasn’t a finished product—it was a bet. Vendors and carriers were spending billions on trials, spectrum plans, and “we’ll scale later” contracts. But scale is a weapon in telecom: once a network gets traction, the compounding effects (users, traffic, recurring revenue) start to feel unstoppable.

From 2014 to 2017, China Mobile climbed from about $61B to $74B. That may sound gradual—until you remember what was happening behind the scenes: spectrum strategy, tower buildouts, and the operational grind of getting new radio deployments right. Meanwhile, infrastructure players like Ericsson and Nokia were moving differently: Ericsson hovered around the mid-teens to low-$20B range, while Nokia’s trajectory bounced as it navigated shifting demand and equipment cycles.

Then the pace changes.
By 2018–2019, China Mobile’s momentum strengthened (roughly $81B → $88B) while Ericsson peaked around $22B–$21B and Nokia pushed into the low-$20Bs. But 2020 becomes the real plot twist: carriers tighten capex, supply chains wobble, and vendor swings turn sharp. Ericsson dips toward ~$19B, and Nokia settles near ~$21B.

From 2021 onward, 5G acceleration rewrites the board. China Mobile surges to about $126B in 2021, then keeps extending its lead, reaching ~$156B by 2025. Ericsson rebounds harder too (up to ~$33B by 2025), while Nokia’s recovery is more uneven—dropping near $18B in 2023 before climbing back to ~$24B.

The dramatic takeaway for the chart race: the “network owner advantage” beats the “vendor cycle advantage” over time.

🔥 Question: If you were investing in the 5G era, would you back the network operators (steady climb) or the infrastructure vendors (bigger swings)? Comment your pick.

facebook_caption:
5G didn’t just improve speeds—it redistributed long-term value across the telecom stack. This chart-race timeline compares China Mobile (network owner scale) with Ericsson and Nokia (infrastructure/vendor exposure), alongside Deutsche Telekom as a benchmark carrier.

Key inflection points: from 2014–2017, China Mobile rises steadily from ~$61B to ~$74B as early 5G preparation turned into execution. In 2018–2019, the infrastructure cycle strengthens (Ericsson around ~$22B and Nokia reaching the low-$20Bs). The shock arrives in 2020: vendor valuations soften (Ericsson down toward ~$19B; Nokia near ~$21B) as telecom spending hesitates.

After 2021, the rollout acceleration favors operators. China Mobile climbs to ~$126B in 2021 and continues compounding to ~$156B by 2025, while Ericsson rebounds into the low-$30Bs and Nokia shows a choppier path—falling toward ~$18B in 2023 before recovering to ~$24B.

Bottom line: the sustained network advantage outlasts the infrastructure boom-and-bust rhythm.
